extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners working on federated learning systems (ML researchers, ML engineers, systems researchers, privacy/fairness researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria, challenges, and desiderata for designing, evaluating, and operating federated learning systems, covering privacy, fairness, robustness, system-induced bias, deployment, runtime, and cross-silo vs cross-device concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy, fairness, and robustness trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the relation between privacy, fairness, and robustness; many works focus on isolated aspects, and an important open challenge is to develop a joint understanding of federated learning systems that are robust, private, and fair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An integrated approach can provide opportunities to benefit from complementary mechanisms (e.g., differential privacy can mitigate inference attacks and provide a foundation for robustness against poisoning) but also reveals new vulnerabilities (e.g., trade-off between privacy and robustness against adversarial examples). Further research needed to characterize tensions and synergies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning representations independent of sensitive attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning data representations that are independent of some sensitive attributes while preserving utility for a task can be motivated by both privacy and fairness objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In centralized settings adversarial training has been used; in federated learning clients could apply transformations locally to enforce privacy/fairness, but learning such a transformation in a federated fashion (potentially under privacy/fairness constraints) is an open problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leveraging federation to improve model diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Federated learning enables integrating datasets previously impractical or illegal to combine (e.g., due to HIPAA/FERPA), offering opportunities to leverage larger, more diverse datasets and improve model generalizability and fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Future research should empirically and theoretically investigate how improving diversity in federated training affects fairness and how differential privacy mechanisms may limit fairness/performance gains from increased diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias in training data (including underrepresentation) as a key consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Bias in training data is a key consideration related to bias and fairness in FL models, particularly due to additional federation-specific sampling steps (e.g., client sampling) and transfer of computation to client devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Underrepresentation in training data is a proven driver of model unfairness (examples cited include genetic disease models and image classification). Designers must consider how federation-specific processes exacerbate or mitigate these effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of sensitive-attribute data complicates fairness measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: The lack of data regarding sensitive attributes in many FL deployments can pose challenges for measuring and ensuring fairness, suggesting reframing fairness problems to avoid requiring such data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research directions include approaches that do not rely on sensitive attribute collection and methods to quantify fairness without direct access to sensitive attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federated fairness: sampling and client-selection biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Federated learning can introduce new sources of bias through decisions about which clients to sample based on connection quality, device type, location, activity patterns, and local dataset size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Future work should investigate the degree to which sampling constraints affect model fairness and explore mitigation approaches (e.g., agnostic federated learning, online fairness frameworks). There is no universally adopted fairness criterion; multiple criteria may be incompatible.

rubrics_metrics.name: System challenges for cross-device deployment
rubrics_metrics.description: Deployment on end-user devices differs from data-center settings due to fleet heterogeneity, limited telemetry, and a requirement that computations not affect device performance or stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addressing these challenges requires extensive automated testing, gradual reversible rollouts with feature flags and A/B experiments, compatibility strategies (stable exchange formats), and significant investment in testing and monitoring infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code deployment and rollout practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Installing, updating and running software on end-user devices often requires extensive manual and automated testing plus gradual reversible rollouts (e.g., server-controlled feature flags) while monitoring metrics like crash rates, memory use, latencies and engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the install base will include various releases, compatibility concerns must be addressed via stable exchange formats or extensive testing; rollouts may take weeks or months and pose particular challenges for devices with spotty connectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring and debugging under privacy constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitoring and debugging are harder because telemetry is limited, delayed, and privacy concerns restrict logging, access, and retention; contributions are anonymous, ephemeral, and available only in aggregate, complicating root-cause analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigations include federated analytics to collect logs privately, training generative models of system behavior for debugging, extensive automated tests, feature flags, and continuous performance monitoring. Reproducing problems in controlled environments is often difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Device availability profiles (Ai(t) and fleet-wide A(t))
rubrics_metrics.description: Device participation is governed by hard constraints (device on, network connectivity, OS permission) and soft constraints (idleness, charging, battery level, unmetered network). These create device-specific, time-varying availability functions Ai(t) and fleet-wide A(t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Availability profiles are often periodic (e.g., daily) and vary by phase/shape/amplitude across devices due to demographics, geography, etc., affecting round completion and participation statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection Bias (due to availability and round mechanics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a device is included in a round depends on its availability profile and the simultaneous number of connected devices; devices active only at fleet-wide peaks or troughs may be under-represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers must account for the interaction between device availability and round-start/selection thresholds to avoid systematic under-representation of certain devices or populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survival Bias (bias toward early/fast reporters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because rounds may be closed once enough devices report, contributions are biased toward devices with better network connections, faster processors, lower CPU load, and less data to process; devices may also drop out due to OS interrupts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigations should consider fairness across devices with varying resource constraints; survival bias can skew aggregate updates toward more performant devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifying bias via expected device contribution rate
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful proxy metric for bias is the expected rate of contribution of a device to federated learning; in an unbiased system this rate would be identical for every device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the non-uniformity of contribution rates to diagnose bias sources; access to realistic device fleet statistics or simulators is a major obstacle for such research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation strategies for system-induced bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible mitigations include early stopping or decreasing model size when contributions correlate with data/model size; post-stratification, stratified sampling, weighting by past contribution profile, sampling without replacement, clustering devices into strata, and changing execution paradigms (e.g., long rounds with many participants and no time-outs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each mitigation has trade-offs: post-stratification requires identifiable strata or proxies; weighting/sampling schemes may be ineffective with very large populations; alternative execution patterns may not be applicable to iterative algorithms. Choice depends on root causes and constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: System parameter tuning as multi-objective optimization
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical federated learning requires balancing multiple potentially conflicting objectives: model quality (loss/accuracy), convergence speed, throughput (rounds, devices), fairness/privacy/robustness, and resource use on server and clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tuning controls (some inherited from datacenter ML, others federated-specific) must account for trade-offs; defining reasonable composite objective functions and algorithms to automatically tune these settings is an open research direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federated-specific controls (clients per round, scheduling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Controls that affect objectives include clients per round (minimum M and number required to start), server-side scheduling (assigning tasks/models to incoming devices), and device-side scheduling (when devices should connect and execute work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Server-side scheduling must balance fairness, starvation avoidance, wait times, and priorities across tenants/tasks. Device-side mechanisms like 'pace steering' can dynamically instruct devices when to return to balance load; designing these under stochastic device availability and feedback loops is challenging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal on-device runtime characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal on-device runtime would be: (1) Lightweight, (2) Performant, (3) Expressive (supporting backprop, control flow, custom extensions), (4) Stable and compact format for data/computations, (5) Widely available (portable open source), (6) Targetable by common ML frameworks/languages, (7) Ideally supports inference or building personalized models for inference runtimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No current solution satisfies all requirements; lack of such runtimes hinders FL adoption. Trade-offs exist between expressiveness and footprint; runtime choices affect compatibility with front-ends like PyTorch/JAX and introduce version skew issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-silo setting operational and heterogeneity concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-silo FL involves fewer, more powerful, and addressable clients, enabling authentication/accounting but raising coordination costs due to heterogeneity in data generation/preprocessing, software stacks/versions, and approval processes across organizations and jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigations include data normalization, standardizing data/model/communication formats (or delivering standardized stacks via containers), and using policy-encoding annotations (e.g., minimum aggregation requirements). Standards efforts (e.g., IEEE P3652.1) are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data partitioning considerations: horizontal vs vertical
rubrics_metrics.description: In cross-device settings data is typically horizontally partitioned (examples share features); in cross-silo settings vertical partitioning (different features across organizations for overlapping entities) is common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vertical partitioning requires entity alignment, handling missing features, and different communication/processing patterns; algorithmic and protocol choices must reflect partitioning type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing, monitoring, and operational investment
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping a federated learning system up and running requires extensive automated continuous test coverage (unit and integration tests), feature flags and A/B rollouts, and continuous monitoring of performance indicators for regressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This investment may be prohibitive for smaller entities; shared and tested infrastructure for FL could reduce costs. Production maintainers are uniquely positioned to provide privacy-preserving fleet statistics for research.
